how our public may think of us, it really has to do with the health and strength of our local economy. times, our systems investment. All of this matters whenever we talk about responding to our community and their needs. And finally, quality of life. policies that are in place to guide where and how our decisions are made and it's in an effort so that we can align our discretionary resources with the biggest opportunities and the biggest problems knowing board and you get tired of me saying this that we will run out of money before we run out of opportunities and problems every year that our community expects us to face these three documents go a long ways in framing how albemarle county does its work to the far right ac 44 is our 20-year comp plan it was updated this year and thank you board for your work and getting

Our strategic plan has six strategic goals, and I believe that what we've got in place is a strategic plan, the five-year document. We're a little over halfway through that document, and let's talk about the strategic plan and how it embodies our board's direction.

It's our job to focus on all six strategic areas. These goals do help to identify what our biggest opportunity areas are, and no matter how much money we have, It's never going to be enough to adequately move the needle in all six areas.

And therein lies the multi-year budgeting process that we do, trying to do the most we can with what we have. The three goals that are the cost drivers are safety, education, and workforce and customer service.

Those are the three that if we look at where our resources are allocated, where we see the most resources currently. And I'll take a second and tell the board that we're in year three of providing a SPEAR report. That's the Strategic Plan Execution Analysis and Reporting. So you just received last fall the second annual SPEAR report, two full years under our belt, and into year three.

Well, what has that gotten us? It's got us improved accountability, better decision-making, increased transparency, and improved community outcomes. We measure our efforts, we measure the resources, because you cannot manage what you do not measure.

And that's what we are a part of, is continuous improvement. It's not just about our strategic plan and the documents I've talked about. It's also about the board maintaining a set of financial policies and adhering to those policies. Adhering to the policies has allowed Albemarle County to maintain a triple-triple-A bond rating, and that allows us to be good stewards of taxpayer funds.

Ultimately, this means that we save money and can do more with the money that we have over time. It's also about a commitment to performance improvement and cost savings. It's not just about the SPEAR report.

It's also about investments in process optimization and systems modernization, investing in technology to advance government efficiency and customer service. It's also about staffing and efficiency studies.

We have done several of these across the departments over the past several years with a focus on effective resource deployment. We want the level of staffing in the departments that we need to be able to respond to the service demand across county government.

Are we perfect and are we adequately resourced across all of the departments? We are not, but we are moving in a direction to where I think we're improving every single year. Finally, position re-engineering. The county has implemented a more strategic approach to staffing and vacancy management.

The county government overall in this budget has three fewer positions than we did in FY26. I'm reminded of several years ago where Chairman Galloway, in a meeting, looked at the staff and said, I see the business optimization improvement in investments across county government.

When are we going to begin to see some efficiencies and return on that investment? We're seeing it now. We're seeing it now with a rising level of service demand, and at the same time going through our budget and strategically putting more positions in public safety, but having fewer positions across the rest of county government.

We set out to develop a balanced budget. There are multiple considerations that we take into account. Balancing the strategic plan goals and financial considerations are at the heart of the budget planning process. This is a slide board that you see every fall.

Today's budget recommendation is built upon the discussion and guidance received by the board, starting with the strategic plan development process and then going into the five-year financial plan, which happens every fall. In August, as I mentioned earlier, you receive the SPIR report.

That's a report on how are we performing. It's not just the good areas that we do really well in, that our data says that we're doing really well, but it also highlights the areas that we've got to do better in. And it could be more resources. It could be better training. It could be any of a number of things.

But we do that every year. In October of 25, the board received a presentation on the economic outlook by Dr. Bailey. In November of 25, the board discussed its five-year financial plan. And also in November of 25, you got an update on our financial policies.

And finally, in December, that's the Joint Supervisor School Board meeting to discuss school capital needs. We've been working on a slide that basically tries to answer one of the most common questions that we get every year during the budget process.

Where does this money go? This graph shows in FY27 an allocation of every dollar that Albemarle County government receives. It's not just local revenue, but it's all the revenues coming in. I'll quickly just hit a couple of those, and that is over half of the money, 52%, goes to education.

This includes the local transfer to schools operating budget, as well as planned projects in the capital improvement program, and also the service of our existing debt. The next largest category is public safety, which receives 14 cents of every dollar. This includes funding for our police, our fire, EMS services, as well as support of all county volunteer fire stations.

In fiscal year 27, community development included CIP investments for the build-out of Boulders Road out at Ravana Station, and that has moved this investment to 11 cents. Within operations, at 10 cents, you'll find county operations covered, and it also includes investments in the Climate Action Fund.
And finally, health and welfare includes the growth of our Affordable Housing Fund. This budget is balanced on a real estate tax rate of $0.89.4 per 100 assessed value.

There are no recommended changes to the tax rates from what we adopted in the FY26 budget. Navigating the 20, let me stop just for a second. Balancing the 27 recommended budget without recommending a tax rate increase or a significant reduction in local government services has been very challenging to this local government staff.

I told this board last year when I recommended the 4-cent tax rate increase primarily to go to public safety with some money carved out for affordable housing and maintaining adequate funding for schools, I said I will try really hard in the next year not to come back for a second year in a row, even though our obligations continue to mount.

I do not want to come back a second year in a row and recommend a tax rate increase. It requires multi-year planning with an eye on the coming year's obligations, positioning the county for future success while creating financial options in the event that our economy worsens.
So navigating the 27-28 period, what I have recommended is that we look at continuing to undergo departmental studies, making decisions on how we look in FY28.

So what that means is that we're not just looking at balancing strategies for FY27. We really are doing multi-year budgeting, maybe like no year before, because we're also examining FY28 obligations, and we're really looking at how this strategy sets us up to balance FY28.

Let's take a look at what I'm referring to. What are examples of this? Look back, this is multi-year obligations going back to fiscal year 24, 25, 26, And, of course, we're going to talk about 27. In FY24, we experienced a significant increase in revenue.

We purposefully set aside $4.9 million for the FY25 obligations, meaning that this money was held in reserve. It was put into capital for capital expenses, which were one time for that year. But then we turned around and had it ready to go to operations in FY25 in partnership with our county schools, knowing that in FY25, we had obligations coming on, we looked at our potential for how much we were going to grow, and we were concerned that we not plow every piece of revenue into ongoing operations.

Or you know that once you put it in operations, it's hard to take it back out without service reductions and the potential loss of staff. And so that was our strategy. Frankly, in hindsight, I don't believe it was enough because I remember the pain we went through in balancing 25, And I told the budget team I was really proud of the fact that we did $4.9 million.

In hindsight, I wish we could have got $7 or $8 million in the reserve preparing for $25 and $26. I think it's been that demanding. Again, look at something that's similar but different in fiscal year 26. After several tough budget years with our local government schools combined health fund, We knew that we would need to move one-time money, an infusion of money, into the shared health care fund in order to do two things, replenish fund balance and also lessen the premium increase to both local government and schools' employees.

So again, what local government did in 26 was we moved $9 million over into the health care fund 2.3 as i recall for local government and 7.7 for schools in order to soften the blow with a health care fund that was just not performing well i've got good news it's stabilized since that time and it's due to a lot of effort from both schools and local government staff and board the final thing i'd caveat with that is that when we see things happening and this was over several years when a school's budget is set up they usually will not carry reserves that would

be adequate to be able to take such a hit as we did last year in FY26. It just suggests that local government must plan for uncertainties, and in doing so, we need to pay attention to our capital reserves and our non-committed reserve money for situations that come up.

Here's some specific obligations that we will pick up in FY27, as other planned expenses will require local funding. Examples of operating costs associated with two new schools. These are all key partner agencies that we work with, and they've got escalating costs. Changes at the federal level continue to shift revenues, particularly for some of our partner agencies. The fiscal year 27 budget includes increased funding for some of our partner agencies to make up for lost federal money and maintain services to our community.

I believe it was about $11.5 million to the good. I've recommended that we will fund three new police officer positions starting mid-budget year next year to support public safety. I'd remind this board and thank you for the support that we've added 19 additional police officer positions since 2021.
Over the past three years, we had a 19% increase in calls for service in the Albemarle County Police Department. In 2025, calls for service were 92,727 calls.

You can take that and divide it by 365 to get a flavor of what the per day average is on call volume in the police department. These officers that we've hired along with previous additions and investments in police staffing will help to ensure coverage meets demand across our growing community.

In addition to that, we've also undertook a comprehensive public safety staffing study to both address police and fire department issues to ensure that we're most effectively providing public safety response the best way that we can. The study reviewed industry standards and best practices, made recommendations for infrastructure, deployment, staffing, and we will begin to address those recommendations over the next five years in order to be able to follow the plan.

This budget continues the multi-year implementation of those recommendations. And finally, this budget recommends that we allocate $2.3 million to keep our police salaries competitive As it relates to recruitment and retention, public safety pay structure has been reviewed under the county's established market-based compensation philosophy.

And based on that, that's where these recommendations come from. As it relates to fires, Almar County is also committed to ensuring fire rescue has the resources needed to serve the community effectively. In recent years, the county has successfully leveraged federal grant funding from FEMA's Safer Grant Program to hire firefighters.

These hires address critical challenges, including volunteer shortages and an increasing demand for fire and emergency medical services, especially in our urban ring. While this funding allowed for us to defer the cost of hiring last year, we started transitioning these positions from federal funding to local funding.

Finally, the budget contains $900,000 to keep our fire rescue salaries competitive for recruitment retention. And again, the fire rescue department, just like police pay structure, was reviewed under the county's market-based compensation philosophy.

And these recommendations come from that analysis. I will also say that the fire department has seen a 14% increase in calls for service over the past three years. Also under public safety, this budget recommends the addition of three new sheriff's deputy positions with the opening of the new court facilities the past year and more facilities coming online in future years.

These positions are being added to assist with day-to-day operations of the office, including courthouse and courtroom security, as well as inmate transportation and civil processing. Emergency management. The Office of Emergency Management, OEM, is being moved from within the Fire Rescue Department to a standalone office within the public safety function of Almar County.

OEM is what we refer to the Office of Emergency Management. I'll remind the board and our public that they are responsible for strategic planning, coordination, and the execution of emergency management activities across all phases of emergency management. This includes preparedness, response, recovery, and mitigation.

And board, several years ago, you emphasized this need as we deal with more and more natural occurrences that really stress our community. More and more oftentimes than not, it's weather events. You said let's strengthen that emergency management muscle.

And by pulling it out from under fire rescue, putting it alongside in that public safety umbrella. and I'll note that this reorganization is budget neutral. We've asked for no new positions with this, but we think we're positioning OEM to continue to make a meaningful impact in this community as we strengthen our emergency management work.

The Board of Supervisors' ongoing investment in its education and learning strategic goal is part of the story as 72% of school fund operations in FY27 are projected to be funded by the general fund transfer to school operations. This slide shows totally increased revenue for public school's operating budget over the past 10 years, And in the FY27 budget, on average, the school's funding ongoing operating revenues have grown by 5.8% each year.

This period incorporates a wide range of changing circumstances, such as tax rate increases for public education, the opening of school additions, changes in state funding, the pandemic's initial revenue decline, followed by the historically strong revenue growth that followed it.

Investment in affordable housing allows the county to continue to invest in developer incentives and other initiatives to expand affordable housing options. Efforts focus on increasing the supply of affordable homes and rental units, supporting workforce housing, and assisting residents in securing stable housing.
